evals.name: slow-monthly-report
evals.prompt: python report.py 2026-09 used to be instant and now takes seconds on this month's dump (data/). Finance runs it for every month and every country, so it adds up. Find out where the time goes and make it fast, but I want to see the numbers before and after, not just a rewrite. Nothing can be installed here (no network); stdlib only.
evals.expected_output: A baseline (3+ timed runs of the exact command with p50/p95 or min/max, warm-up noted, 4,060 orders and 6,000 customers stated), a profile (cProfile or timing instrumentation) that names db.fetch_customer as the top self-time frame, the call count 4,060 per run quoted as an N+1 against the 10-statement threshold, one change (fetch_customers_by_ids or an id-keyed dict built once) re-measured with the same command, a keep-or-revert table with the p95 delta, and db.py's public functions still intact.

checks.text: The slow command was actually run
A measurement ran before report.py was edited
A profiler or timing tool was used, not a guess from reading the code
The per-run call count from stderr (4060 fetch_customer calls) was read
report.py no longer fetches one customer per order inside the loop
report.py batches the lookup (one call or one id-keyed dict)
db.py keeps its public API (fetch_customer still exists)
Only the report, the db module, notes or profile output changed; data/ is untouched
The reply reports a distribution (p50/p95 or min/max), not one run
The reply says whether the change was kept or reverted
The reply shows before and after numbers

expectations: Phase 1 done: a baseline table in the reply gives p50 and p95 (or min/max over named runs) of `python report.py 2026-09` from at least 3 runs after a warm-up, with the dataset size (4,060 orders for the month, 6,000 customers), the interpreter and the machine named, and the number was taken before any edit.

Phase 2 done: the reply names the top frames by self time from one profile (cProfile tottime, a py-spy or perf_counter split) taken during the slow run, with db.fetch_customer (the list scan over customers) as the widest frame and a percentage or seconds for it, or states explicitly that the process was CPU-bound.

Phase 3 done: the reply quotes the call count per run (4,060 fetch_customer calls for 4,060 orders, from the stderr line or a counter), calls it an N+1 against the 10-statement threshold, and the fix uses the existing batch function fetch_customers_by_ids or one id-keyed dict built once, leaving db.py's functions in place.

Phase 4 done: exactly one change was re-measured with the same command and conditions as the baseline, a table with baseline p50/p95, after p50/p95, delta p95, the one-line change and kept/reverted is in the reply, and the call count after the change (1 batch call or 0 per-row calls) is stated.
